abstract: We address the implementation of public policies (alternatives) when the feasible set is unknown to the planner. The implementing agents are the political parties, who know the feasible set. They care about the implemented alternative, which reflects their ideology, and their share in parliament and office. They face a mechanism that, given the alternatives proposed by all parties, asks the voters to rank them and determines the chosen alternative and the shares in parliament and office. We identify conditions on parties’ preferences that guarantee the socially optimal policy is the outcome of the unique pure strategy Nash equilibrium of the electoral game played by the parties. The existence of the equilibrium does not require any assumptions about the parties’ ideology. To ensure uniqueness, shares must prevail over ideology: office or parliamentary shares in two-party systems, and strictly office shares in systems with more than two parties.
title: Implementation via political parties

abstract: Recent disruptions to global oil markets, from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine to the war in Iran, have revived fears of stagflation. This column shows that the shale revolution has fundamentally changed how the US economy responds to oil shocks. As the country has shifted from a major petroleum importer to a net exporter, adverse oil supply news has become considerably less contractionary and can even support activity, with benefits extending beyond the oil sector. The findings suggest that the Federal Reserve faces a more favourable trade-off between activity and inflation, even as households and firms remain exposed to higher energy costs.
authors: Diego Känzig, James Stock, Luca Zanotti
